blocks.text: Counting possibilities without listing every one rests on the multiplication principle: if a first step can be carried out in m ways and, after each of them, a second step can be carried out in n ways, the two steps together can be carried out in m × n ways. The same rule extends to any number of steps in sequence. When n distinct items are placed in a row with no item repeated, there are n choices for the first place, n − 1 remaining choices for the second, and so on down to 1 for the last. That product of all whole numbers from n down to 1 is called the factorial of n and written n!; by definition, 0! = 1.

Often only r items are selected from n distinct items, again without repeating any item. Whether two selections count as different then depends on whether the order of the chosen items matters. An ordered selection of r items from n distinct items is called a permutation, and its count is written P(n, r). Filling r places in order multiplies r descending factors starting at n, which factorials write compactly as

Dividing n! by (n − r)! cancels the factors for the n − r items left out. When all n items are arranged in order, r equals n and P(n, n) = n! ÷ 0! = n!. For 4 distinct items taken 2 at a time, P(4, 2) = 4! ÷ 2! = 4 × 3 = 12.

An unordered selection of r items from n distinct items is called a combination, and its count is written C(n, r). Here rearranging the same r chosen items does not create a new outcome: a committee of three members with equal duties is the same committee whichever member is named first. Each combination of r items yields r! different permutations once those r items are placed in every possible order, so P(n, r) = C(n, r) × r!, giving

For 4 items taken 2 at a time, C(4, 2) = 12 ÷ 2! = 6. Every choice of r items to take is also a choice of n − r items to leave behind, so C(n, r) always equals C(n, n − r). Table 1 compares P(n, 3) and C(n, 3) for pools of 5 to 8 distinct items.

blocks.text: Software often needs to check whether a sequence of characters, called a string, follows a pattern: whether an input holds only digits, or whether brackets open in the expected order. A deterministic finite state machine, also called a deterministic finite automaton, is a simple model that performs such checks using a fixed, finite set of states. The symbols allowed in the input form a finite set called the input alphabet.

Before reading any input, the machine sits in one designated start state. It then reads the input string one symbol at a time from left to right without changing the string. A rule called the transition function tells the machine which state to enter next from its current state and the symbol just read. The machine is called deterministic because for every state and every symbol in the alphabet, the transition function specifies one and only one next state: no step is missing and no step offers a choice.

Zero, one or more of the states are marked as accepting states, also called final states. Once the last symbol of the string has been read, the string is accepted if the machine finishes in an accepting state, and rejected otherwise. Passing through an accepting state earlier in the string is not enough: only the state at the very end counts. If the input is the empty string, which contains zero symbols, the machine makes no transitions at all and finishes in the start state, so the empty string is accepted if and only if the start state itself is accepting.

A machine can be shown either as a transition diagram or as a transition table. In a diagram each state is a circle, an arrow entering from outside marks the start state, a double circle marks each accepting state, and labelled arrows show the transitions. A non-accepting state whose transitions for every symbol loop back to itself is called a trap state: once the machine enters it, no later symbols can lead out. Figure 1 and Table 1 show the same machine M over the alphabet {0, 1}. On 100 it moves q₀ → q₁ → q₂ → q₂ and accepts; on 101 it moves q₀ → q₁ → q₂ → q₁ and rejects.

blocks.alt: A state diagram with four states q₀, q₁, q₂ and q₃. Start arrow enters q₀. State q₂ has a double circle marking it as the only accepting state. Transitions: from q₀, 0 loops to q₀ and 1 goes to q₁; from q₁, 0 goes to q₂ and 1 goes to q₃; from q₂, 0 loops to q₂ and 1 goes to q₁; from q₃, both 0 and 1 loop to q₃.

blocks.text: Ecologists track how a population of size N changes over time by comparing births and deaths. The population growth rate is the net number of individuals added per unit of time, and the per-capita growth rate is that rate divided by N, the average net contribution per individual. When food, space and other resources are abundant, each individual reproduces and survives at a constant net per-capita rate r, called the intrinsic rate of increase. Under this exponential growth model, the population growth rate is
exponential growth rate = r × N

Because r stays constant while N rises, a positive r makes the population add more individuals in each successive time interval than in the one before. Plotted against time, N follows a steepening J-shaped curve that grows without bound.

No natural environment supplies unlimited resources forever. The carrying capacity K is the maximum population size that a particular environment can sustain indefinitely. The logistic growth model accounts for limited resources by multiplying the exponential rate by (K − N) ÷ K, the fraction of the carrying capacity still unused:
logistic growth rate = r × N × (K − N) ÷ K

Dividing this expression by N shows that the logistic per-capita growth rate is r × (K − N) ÷ K. When N is very small compared with K, (K − N) ÷ K is close to 1 and logistic growth is nearly exponential. As N grows, competition for scarce resources lowers the per-capita rate. Total individuals added per unit of time rise at first because N is growing, reach a maximum at N = K ÷ 2 (half the carrying capacity), and then fall as (K − N) ÷ K shrinks towards zero.

At N = K, births and deaths balance, the growth rate is zero, and the curve levels off, forming an S-shaped curve from a small start. If a population ever starts or is pushed above K, then K − N is negative, making the growth rate negative so that N declines towards K. Figure 1 compares exponential and logistic trajectories starting from the same initial size with the same positive r.

blocks.text: Toothed wheels, or gears, transmit rotation from a driving (input) shaft to a driven (output) shaft without slipping. For two external gears to mesh smoothly, their teeth must have the same spacing around the rim, so each gear’s effective radius is proportional to its number of teeth N. Where the two rims meet they push each other in the same tangential direction, which makes external gears in direct contact turn in opposite senses: if the input gear turns clockwise, the gear meshing with it turns anticlockwise.

Because teeth pass the point of contact one for one, a gear with more teeth completes fewer revolutions in a given time. With N_in and N_out for the tooth counts of the input and output gears, and ω_in and ω_out for their rotational speeds (measured in revolutions per minute, rev/min, or radians per second, rad/s), the gear ratio R is
R = N_out ÷ N_in = ω_in ÷ ω_out

Rearranging gives ω_out = ω_in ÷ R: when a small gear drives a larger gear, R is greater than 1 and rotational speed drops. Turning effort on a shaft is measured by torque τ, in newton metres (N·m). Rotational power, in watts (W), is torque times angular speed in rad/s. In an ideal gear train with negligible friction, all input power reaches the output, so slowing the shaft multiplies its torque by the same ratio R:
τ_out ÷ τ_in = ω_in ÷ ω_out = N_out ÷ N_in

When an intermediate gear on its own shaft sits between the input and output gears and meshes with both, without delivering power to its own shaft, it is called an idler gear. Across the two meshes, R = (N_idler ÷ N_in) × (N_out ÷ N_idler) = N_out ÷ N_in: the idler’s tooth count cancels out, leaving output speed and torque unchanged while reversing the direction a second time so input and output turn the same way. To multiply ratios instead, a compound gear train fixes two gears of different tooth counts rigidly onto the same intermediate shaft so both turn together; the overall gear ratio is then the product of the stage ratios, R_total = R₁ × R₂. Figure 1 shows a three-gear train drawn on its effective circles.

blocks.text: Projects such as fitting out a laboratory or launching a product consist of separate activities, some of which can run in parallel while others depend on earlier work. In a finish-to-start dependency, an activity cannot begin until every one of its immediate predecessors has finished. The critical path method (CPM) maps these dependencies in an activity network — boxes for activities and arrows from predecessors to successors — to find the shortest time in which the whole project can finish and where the schedule has room for delay.

With d for an activity’s duration, a forward pass works from start to finish to find each activity’s earliest start (ES) and earliest finish (EF). Activities with no predecessors start at time 0, so ES = 0. Where one or more predecessors lead into an activity, all of them must finish first, so ES equals the largest EF among its immediate predecessors. Adding the duration gives
EF = ES + d

The largest EF among the ending activities is the minimum completion time of the entire project. A backward pass then works from finish back to start to find each activity’s latest finish (LF) and latest start (LS) — the latest times it can finish and start without delaying that project completion time. An activity with no successors has LF equal to the project completion time; an activity followed by one or more immediate successors has LF equal to the smallest LS among those successors, and
LS = LF − d
The scheduling leeway of an activity is called its slack, or float:
slack = LS − ES = LF − EF

A path from start to finish with the longest total duration is called a critical path; a project may have one critical path or more than one tied for the longest duration. When LF at the end is set to the minimum project completion time, every activity on a critical path has zero slack: delaying it delays the whole project. Shortening the project requires shortening activities on the critical path, and cutting a critical activity far enough can make another path take over as critical. blocks.text: In many markets, the buyers and sellers bear all the costs and receive all the benefits of their trade. Sometimes, however, producing or consuming a good affects a third party, someone who neither buys nor sells it, without compensation. Economists call such a spillover effect an externality. A negative externality imposes a cost on third parties, as when a dye factory releases waste into a river used by downstream fisheries. A positive externality gives third parties an unpaid benefit, as when a vaccinated resident makes neighbours less likely to catch an illness.

To compare what a market does on its own with what is best for everyone together, costs and benefits are measured for one additional unit, that is, on the margin. The marginal private cost (MPC) is what producers pay to make one more unit, such as wages and materials. The marginal external cost (MEC) is the damage that extra unit causes to third parties. Their sum is the marginal social cost (MSC), the full cost to society of one more unit:
MSC = MPC + MEC

On the demand side, the marginal private benefit (MPB) is the most buyers are willing to pay for one more unit, and the marginal external benefit (MEB) is the gain to third parties. Their sum is the marginal social benefit (MSB):
MSB = MPB + MEB

Left to itself, a competitive market settles where MPB equals MPC, because buyers and sellers weigh only their own gains and expenses. Society as a whole does best at the socially efficient quantity, where MSB equals MSC. When MEC is positive and MEB is zero, MSC lies above MPC while MSB equals MPB, so an unregulated market produces more than the socially efficient quantity. When MEB is positive and MEC is zero, MSB lies above MPB while MSC equals MPC, so an unregulated market produces too little.

The economist Arthur Pigou proposed correcting an externality with a tax or subsidy per unit. For a negative externality, this Pigouvian (or corrective) tax is set equal to the marginal external cost at the socially efficient quantity:
corrective tax per unit = MEC at the socially efficient quantity

Because producers must pay this tax on every unit, their private marginal cost rises by the tax, so they internalise the external cost at the margin and the market settles where MSB equals MSC. Even when MEC grows with output, as in Figure 1, a constant per-unit tax equal to MEC at the socially efficient quantity brings the market to that quantity. For a positive externality, a corrective subsidy per unit equal to MEB at the socially efficient quantity raises output to where MSB equals MSC.

blocks.text: In reliability engineering, the reliability R of a component over a stated operating period, such as one year of continuous service, is the probability that it performs its function throughout that period without failing. As a probability, R lies from 0 to 1, and the probability that the component fails during the period is F = 1 − R. Throughout this passage, component failures are statistically independent: whether one part fails does not alter the probability that any other part fails.

Engineers represent how parts depend on one another with a reliability block diagram. The diagram shows logical dependence rather than physical wiring: the system succeeds whenever at least one unbroken path of working blocks connects the input (In) to the output (Out).

Components stand in series when every one of them must work for the system to work, so the first component failure stops the system. For n independent components with reliabilities R1, R2, …, Rn in series, the system reliability is their product:
R_series = R1 × R2 × … × Rn
Because multiplying by a number below 1 makes a positive value smaller, adding an imperfect part in series always lowers reliability below that of the weakest part in the chain.

To guard against failure, engineers add redundancy by placing components in parallel. In active parallel redundancy, all branches operate and the group succeeds as long as at least one branch works; it fails only when every branch fails during the period. For independent branches, the failure probability of the parallel group is the product of the individual failure probabilities:
Subtracting this combined failure probability from 1 gives the reliability of the parallel group:

Adding a parallel branch always raises reliability above that of the single most reliable branch in the group. A diagram that mixes series and parallel sections is solved in stages: replace each parallel group with one equivalent block carrying its R_parallel, then multiply along the series chain. Figure 1 shows the block diagram of a furnace cooling-water line over one year: water must pass through Filter A and be driven by at least one of the two pumps, B or C.

blocks.text: Social scientists classify goods and shared resources along two dimensions. A good is excludable if it is practical to stop people who have not paid, or who lack permission, from using it; it is non-excludable if, once supplied, nobody nearby can reasonably be kept from benefiting. A good is rivalrous if one person's use leaves less of it for others, and non-rivalrous if one person's use does not diminish anyone else's ability to use it at the same time.

Crossing these two criteria produces the four categories in Table 1. A loaf of bread is a private good: a shop can withhold it until paid, and eating it leaves none for anyone else. An encrypted weather-data feed is a club good: a password keeps non-subscribers out, yet one subscriber reading the forecast takes nothing from another. Wild fish in open coastal waters are a common-pool resource: boats are hard to keep out, while every fish landed leaves one fewer in the water. Flood defences protecting a valley and street lighting are public goods: they protect or light the way for everyone there at once, payers and non-payers alike.

blocks.text: In this framework, calling something a public good describes how it is consumed, not who pays for it. A city council may hand out rivalrous, excludable items such as school meals, which remain private goods, whereas a private broadcaster may supply free-to-air radio — non-excludable and non-rivalrous — by selling advertisements alongside it. Conditions also matter: an untolled highway is non-excludable and non-rivalrous late at night, when extra cars slow nobody down, whereas during a traffic jam road space becomes rivalrous, turning the same road into a common-pool resource.

Providing a public good or conserving a common-pool resource requires collective action, in which group members contribute money, effort or restraint toward a shared benefit. Because a public good is non-excludable, an individual can hope to free ride: enjoy what others pay for while contributing nothing. When one member's contribution costs more than the extra benefit that contribution alone brings back to that member, self-interest pushes each member to hold back, even though all members would be better off if everyone contributed. This free-rider problem can end in under-provision, where some contribute and others free ride, or in non-production, where everyone holds back so the good is never produced at all and nobody has anything to free ride on. Common-pool resources face a parallel trap of overuse, because each user keeps the full gain of taking an extra unit while sharing the depletion cost with the whole group. Groups and governments address both problems through compulsory taxes, enforceable quotas, community monitoring with penalties, or tying excludable member benefits to contributions.

blocks.text: In linguistics, morphology studies the internal structure of words and how words are built. Although a word can stand on its own as an utterance, many words contain smaller meaningful parts. A morpheme is the smallest systematic pairing of a form (a spoken sound or sign) with a meaning or grammatical function. The English word "cats" contains two morphemes: "cat", naming the animal, and "-s", marking plural number.

A free morpheme can stand alone as a word, such as "cat", "kind" or "teach", whereas a bound morpheme appears only when attached to another morpheme. The indivisible core morpheme of a word is its root, while any unit to which another morpheme attaches — a bare root or one already carrying other pieces — is a base. Bound morphemes that attach to a base are affixes: a prefix precedes its base ("un-" in "unkind"), a suffix follows it ("-ness" in "kindness"), and an infix is inserted inside a root. A suffix sitting between a root and a later suffix, like "-y" in "unluckiness", remains a suffix rather than an infix. Every affix is bound, though not every bound morpheme is an affix: English has bound roots such as "-whelm" in "overwhelm", and in several languages most verb roots are bound.

Derivational affixes build new words and select the word category (such as noun, verb or adjective) of their base. Derivational suffixes often change category — "-ness" turns adjectives into nouns, and "-ly" turns adjectives into adverbs — whereas English derivational prefixes alter meaning without changing category. Because each affix attaches to the outer edge of a base of the category it selects, order is fixed: in "foolishly", "-ish" first turns the noun "fool" into an adjective so "-ly" has an adjective base. Inflectional affixes, by contrast, never change the word category of their base or coin a new word; they mark grammatical properties required by a sentence, such as plural "-s" or past-tense "-ed".

Compounding joins two or more roots rather than a root and an affix. English spells compounds solid ("sunflower"), hyphenated ("kind-hearted") or with a space ("bus stop"), so linguists identify them by stress and syntax rather than spaces. Most English compounds are endocentric: their rightmost member is the head, fixing both word category and the kind of thing meant, so a "bluebird" is a kind of bird. Exocentric compounds lack this internal semantic head: a "spoilsport" is a person who ruins fun, not a kind of sport.

options.text: An inflectional affix can stand alone as a word, whereas a derivational affix is always bound.
options.why: All affixes attach to a base and are bound morphemes; neither inflectional nor derivational affixes stand alone.

options.text: An inflectional affix always precedes its base, whereas a derivational affix always follows it.
options.why: Preceding or following a base distinguishes prefixes from suffixes; English inflectional affixes such as "-s" and "-ed" are suffixes.

options.text: An inflectional affix expresses grammatical information and never changes the word category of its base.
options.why: This is the contrast stated at the end of the third paragraph.

options.text: An inflectional affix joins two roots together, whereas a derivational affix attaches to one root.

options.text: The suffix "-ness" in "sharpness", formed from the adjective "sharp".
options.why: "-ness" turns the adjective "sharp" into a noun, changing word category: a derivational suffix.

options.text: The suffix "-ish" in "childish", formed from the noun "child".
options.why: "-ish" turns the noun "child" into an adjective, coining a new word of a different category: a derivational suffix.

options.text: The suffix "-er" in "teacher", formed from the verb "teach" to name a person.
options.why: "-er" turns the verb "teach" into an agent noun, changing category and core meaning: a derivational suffix.

options.text: The suffix "-ed" in "painted", formed from the verb "paint" to mark past tense.
options.why: Past-tense "-ed" adds grammatical tense while leaving "paint" a verb: an inflectional suffix.

questions.explanation: A compound combines two or more roots, and it is exocentric when it lacks an internal semantic head — that is, when it does not name a subtype of its right-hand member. "Pickpocket" names a thief, not a pocket; "bookshelf" and "greenhouse" are endocentric, and "helpfulness" is formed by derivation, not compounding.

options.text: "Pickpocket", naming a thief who steals valuables from people's pockets, built from "pick" and "pocket".
options.why: It joins two roots ("pick" and "pocket"), yet the whole word denotes a person rather than a subtype of its right-hand member "pocket".

options.text: "Bookshelf", naming a wooden or metal shelf made for holding books, built from "book" and "shelf".
options.why: A bookshelf is a kind of shelf, so its right-hand member serves as its semantic and category head: an endocentric compound.

options.text: "Greenhouse", naming a heated glass house used for growing plants, built from "green" and "house".
options.why: Although not green in colour, a greenhouse is still a kind of house (structure), so its right-hand member heads an endocentric compound.

options.text: "Helpfulness", naming the personal quality of being helpful, built from "help", "-ful" and "-ness".
options.why: "Helpfulness" contains one root ("help") and two derivational suffixes, so it is a derived word rather than a compound.

questions.explanation: The second paragraph explicitly distinguishes bound roots from affixes: every affix is bound because it must attach to a base, whereas bound roots (like "-whelm" in "overwhelm") are bound morphemes that are roots rather than affixes.

options.text: Any affix standing between a root and a later suffix inside a word, like "-ful" in "carefulness", is an infix.
options.why: "-ful" attaches after the root "care" and is followed by "-ness", so it remains a suffix; an infix must be inserted inside a single root.

options.text: Every affix is a bound morpheme, whereas not every bound morpheme in a language is an affix.
options.why: All affixes must attach to a base, while bound roots (such as "-whelm" in "overwhelm") are also bound without being affixes.

options.text: Two roots separated by a space in English spelling, such as "bus stop", cannot form a compound word.
options.why: The fourth paragraph notes that English spells some compounds with spaces, so spaces alone do not rule out compounding.

options.text: Derivational prefixes in English regularly change the word category of the base they attach to.
options.why: The third paragraph states the opposite: derivational prefixes in English alter meaning without changing the base's word category.

questions.explanation: In English endocentric compounds the head stands on the right and determines both word category and the kind of thing meant. Both "boat" and "house" are nouns, so both compounds are nouns, while reversing their order shifts the head — and thus the kind of object named — from a kind of boat ("houseboat") to a kind of house ("boathouse").

options.text: The word category shifts from a noun to an adjective, while the word still refers to a kind of boat.
options.why: Both roots are nouns, so the right-hand member remains a noun in both orders, and the head shifts from "boat" to "house".

options.text: Neither category nor core meaning changes, because an endocentric compound weights both roots equally.
options.why: In English endocentric compounds only the rightmost member is the head; the left member modifies it.

options.text: The word ceases to be a compound and becomes an inflected plural or tense form of the root "boat".
options.why: Reversing two roots still combines two roots, which is compounding rather than inflection.

options.text: The word category stays a noun, while the core meaning shifts from a kind of boat to a kind of house.
options.why: The rightmost root is the head in English: "boat" heads "houseboat" (a boat for living in), whereas "house" heads "boathouse" (a shelter for boats).

questions.explanation: Each derivational affix attaches to a base of the category it selects. Starting from the verb "build", attaching "re-" first produces the verb "rebuild", and "-able" can then select that verb base to produce the adjective "rebuildable". In the reverse order, "-able" would first turn "build" into the adjective "buildable", leaving an adjective base to which verb-selecting "re-" cannot attach.

options.text: "-able" attaches to "build" first to form the adjective "buildable", and "re-" then attaches to that adjective.
options.why: Once "-able" turns "build" into the adjective "buildable", "re-" can no longer attach because "re-" selects only verbs.

options.text: Either order works, because a prefix and a suffix attach to opposite edges of the root without interacting.
options.why: Each affix selects the category of the entire base it attaches to, so changing the base from a verb to an adjective blocks "re-".

options.text: "re-" attaches to "build" first to form the verb "rebuild", since "-able" first would yield an adjective "re-" cannot take.
options.why: Attaching "re-" to the verb "build" yields the verb base "rebuild", which still satisfies "-able"'s requirement for a verb base.

options.text: "re-" and "-able" first join each other into a single affix, which then attaches to the verb root "build" at once.
options.why: "re-" and "-able" are independent derivational affixes that occur separately (as in "rebuild" and "buildable"), each attaching step by step.
